avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Rage' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of this profile and trauma type. For life-threatening illness, the other items center on bodily threat, fragmented/sensory illness memories, restricted safety, and avoidance. A fear of losing control and doing something terrible reflects an anger/aggression concern that is not supported elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Maladaptive Strategies, making it feel clinically mismatched rather than just unusual.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is relatively weakly anchored to the rest of this illness-based profile. The other items emphasize body-focused threat, limited safe places, inability to relax, and sensory/body memory phenomena. Hypervigilance to loud or unexpected sounds is more typical of external danger trauma and is not clearly connected to the appraisals or strategies selected here, so this item stands out as poorly integrated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' fits interpersonal or preventable external trauma better than life-threatening illness. For a 39-year-old nurse with illness trauma, this appraisal is hard to reconcile unless there is a strong medical-blame narrative, which is otherwise not represented in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
issues.explanation: 'I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred' is more characteristic of discrete external traumatic incidents with a specific body posture during the event. In life-threatening illness, this can occur, but alongside the rest of this profile it is less coherent than illness-linked sensory or somatic memory items and stands out as a poor fit.
